title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 3-8
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose tells the story of Shitou's childhood from Richard McDaniel's Zen Masters of China, then takes up lines three through eight of the Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage. On the weeds that appear once the hut is finished, Joden offers a gardener's fable, Suzuki Roshi's teaching that weeds become nourishment, and Sojun Mel Weitsman's commentary on Dogen's line about blossoms and weeds. Participants then consider the shift from "I" to "the person in the hut," a Diamond Sutra line about dwelling nowhere, and Satchel Paige's remark that the social ramble ain't restful. Breakout rooms take up where we actually live, and the session closes with the four vows.
topics: natural cycle of birth and death

sentences.text: **Joden Bob Rose:** So I realized I was muted for that, but I'm sure you can hear yourselves chanting this wonderful poem.
As I promised, each week I try to give a little background about Shurdu.
So here's a story from a book called Zen Masters of China by Richard McDaniel.
*Shurdu was born in Gaiao, which at that time was a very primitive area.
He was described as being a well-behaved and generous child who was bright and self-confident beyond his years.
Orthodox Buddhists attributed these traits to the fact that his mother, contrary to local custom, chose to refrain from eating meat during her pregnancy.
Many of the people in Gaiao still lived in caves and worshiped the old gods who demanded sacrifices of wine and cattle.

From an early age, Shurdu was skeptical of the value of these practices, so he desecrated the shrines in order to see if the supposed gods would retaliate, which they didn't, and he freed the cattle from their pens.*
*Stories about the six patriarch had reached even this backwater, and when he was 13 years old, Shurdu traveled to Baolin to become Huineng's disciple.
The patriarch died within a year, and among the monks gathered around Huineng, Shurdu asked him, "Master, what should I do?"
"You should go to Qingzhi," Huineng instructed him, but Shurdu misunderstood him to say Qingzhi, or seek thoughts.
Shurdu interpreted this to mean he should observe his thoughts during the practice of meditation, a technique advocated by certain teachers of the day.*
*Seeking to follow what he understood to be Huineng's advice, he dedicated himself to sitting in meditation, observing his thoughts as they rose and passed away.
One day, an older disciple of Huineng asked him how he was practicing.
"I'm following our master's instructions, I'm observing the rise and fall of my thoughts."
The older monk gently suggested that Shurdu may have misunderstood the six patriarch and told him he should go seek out the master's heir, Qingwan, Qingzhi.
Qingwan had several monks studying with him, but when Shurdu presented himself, the master remarked, "I have many cattle with two horns among my followers."*
So that's our story of Shurdu for tonight.
Next week I will tell the story about his encounter with his master.
So first of all, we discussed the first two lines last week and asked you to take some notes and have some reflections.
Anyone have a comment they'd like to offer about the opening of this poem we're studying?
And Hanna's going to handle putting you on the screen.
Well, if you just put in speaker view, that would be automatic.
**Participant:** I have a question about the word "where" in the first line.
It says, "I built a grass hut where there's nothing of value."

Does that mean the hut is built where there's nothing of value, or does it mean there's nothing of value in the hut, which is how Ben Connelly seems to interpret it, but the English doesn't quite work?
**Joden Bob Rose:** No, and in fact, as I mentioned last week, nothing of value, the character is the character Mu.
Robert, is there anything different in your computer setup that you're cutting out?
I don't think so.
Okay.
We'll just trust in the gods.
I missed most of what you said.
The character for nothing is Wu or Mu.
And so one could read this as "I've built a hut empty of value" or "entirely without value," without even specifying a location.
It's my understanding.
Other comments or thoughts?
Now I'll just ask you, if you want to talk, unmute yourself and put yourself on speaker view.
Do you know how to do that?
You don't have to do it, Bob.
The person who's talking.
All right.
So I'm unmuted.
You're unmuted.
Okay.
So any other comments before we dive into lines three and four and then four through six, or five through eight, I should say?
**Participant:** I just wanted to mention how perfectly beautiful the introduction is by Ben Connelly.
He was so generous, and "be present when you read this book.
It's good for your present.
Meet the poem with interaction based on wellness and a generous way of being."
It was just so bountiful.
The way he asked one to be while reading this book was just perfectly beautiful.
And I'm trying to do that too.
**Joden Bob Rose:** As we all should.
Yeah.
So don't miss the introduction.
So lines three and four.
I should say that today we're going to have six lines because we only did two the first week.
But in the future, mostly we'll have four lines to contemplate.
These lines: when it was completed, fresh weeds appeared.
Now it's been lived in, covered by weeds.
We talked the other day about what this hut means or represents.
One of the early metaphors in Buddhism, and the Buddha speaks in the Dhammapada where he makes this being the hut, our mind, quite explicit, when he says:
*As rain leaks into a poorly roofed house, so does passion invade an uncultivated mind.*
So in this case, we're dealing with a house that's just been built, but these weeds show up.
So it immediately raises the question: what are weeds?
What is a weed?
A couple of thoughts here.
There's a fable that tells of a gardener who tried everything to get rid of the weeds in his garden.
And he couldn't do it.
In exasperation, he contacts a famous expert who inquires whether he's attempted a variety of remedies.
When the gardener replies he's tried all of them, the expert pauses and reflects and finally replies, "Well, all I can suggest is that you learn to love the weeds."
Our teacher Suzuki Roshi in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind has a lovely passage.
And he says:
*When pulling out the weeds, we give nourishment to the plant.
We should rather be grateful for the weeds because eventually they will enrich your practice.
If you have some experience of how the weeds in your mind change into mental nourishment, your practice will make remarkable progress.
You will feel the progress.
You will feel how they change into self nourishment.
We must have the actual experience of how our weeds change into nourishment.*
Other commentators and people have thought about this and say, well, think about our bodies.
The weeds are our aches and our pains.
They're evidence of our mortality.
And our thoughts certainly are like weeds.
They just show up.
They keep emerging.
And our practice really helps us understand that they're neither good nor bad.
It's interesting, again, having the benefit of looking this poem over with my Chinese scholar friend Paul Hanson, that the first character in this line means "completed."
So he was saying completed this hut, but it's made of grass.
So is it completed?
It's only completed in this moment because he clearly knows that it's going to break down and decay.
But then the next line, the first character starts with "ruin."
So he begins to say completed and immediately it's ruined.
So in a sense, these two lines are really about the whole cycle of coming and going, of emerging and decaying, of the whole cycle of life and our lives.

Just for our benefit, I've also looked at some other alternative translations besides the Kazuaki Tanahashi, Daniel Leighton, and James Mitchell, another translator, translates these lines as "the grass thatching still looks new.
When it wears out, I'll add fresh thatch to the roof."
And what's interesting, again, the Chinese characters: the character for thatch, it's pronounced mao, and the character for all grasses is chow.
And so in the poem, the distinction is made between the grass for thatch and all other grasses.
**Participant:** I think what was important for me, what came up, was on page, in chapter four, on page 36, regarding what we're talking about.
And in there, he talks about, here's what we do with the weeds that keep coming up: is to practice to be with the weeds.
And it occurred to me, just when I read that in a couple other similar sentences, that I keep saying, "Oh, I'm overwhelmed.
There's too much that comes up that I don't know what to do with."
And when I read this, all of a sudden, that dissipated.
And that said, you know, practice to be here with the weeds.
And I just wanted to mention just how one little phrase can twist a whole line of thinking into more positive.
**Participant:** I can add to what Janet was saying about the weeds.
I was watching my reactions today at the inauguration, which I probably spent way too much time watching, but it was wonderful.
And looking at how I felt on January 6, and then looking again at how I was feeling today, and thinking, well, am I supposed to be equanimous?
And I was really, you know, this whole period of time, people have died, and I've been sad.
And then something uplifting happens, and I've been joyful.

And I have really been appreciating my weeds, because they've really been putting me in touch with the feelings, some of the sadness, some of the anger, and all those feelings that other people have been going through.
And I feel a real connection to both sides of this, all the stuff that we're going through.
So I'm glad to have my weeds, and I've learned a lot from them, and I hope I continue to have them.
**Joden Bob Rose:** You can't get away without them.
No, I think really the point of that passage I read earlier is no matter how hard you try to kill the weeds, they still keep coming.
There's no avoiding their emergence.
And it's sobering to think the thistle seed lasts for 100 years in the soil.
So no matter how hard you try, they're still going to keep coming back.
**Participant:** I have a couple of things that I want to say.
One is as a gardener.
Somebody once sent me one of those kitchen magnets, and I think it's relevant here.
As a gardener, your first mistake is to think that you're in control.
And the other is the definition of a weed: it's something that you don't want in your garden.
And we all have these different definitions of what a weed is.
And, you know, when you think about it, people eat dandelion leaves, right?
While the rest of us are trying to get them all out of our garden.
So just seeing those, bringing our preferences, bringing our likes and our dislikes to whatever our definition of weeds is, if we can just leave those behind, it makes such a big difference.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Someone pointed out, those of you who have been reading Connelly's book, one of his commentaries is that Shurdu hasn't created some ideal weed-free realm.
He's here with what keeps coming up, to practice with the weeds of delusion, the weeds of difficulty.

Chris Burkhart, a couple of Sundays ago, gave a really great talk about how we need the uneasiness and discomfort of delusion to fully accept the dukkha of our lives, to be on this continual path of transformation and growth.
So if we see weeds as obstacles, they're obstacles.
If we see them as weeds, they aren't obstacles.
It's, again, how our minds make sense or not of the phenomena of the world.

In kind of figuring out this talk, I came across a passage I'd like to read you, and it's an homage because Sojun Mel Weitsman passed away, I think, last week, and a great teacher for many people in this lineage.
And he's reflecting on Dogen's line that we chant in our Saturday service from the Genjokoan:
*Yet in attachment blossoms fall and in aversion weeds spring up.*
So Mel's commentary on this is:
*In Zazen, we are continually confronted with aversion and attachment.
We want something nice.
We all want something pleasant, something that feels good, a wonderful state of mind.
Sometimes when we have a wonderful state of mind with no pain, we think, "Ah, this is it.
This is great.
This is all worth it.
That's why I'm here."
But as soon as we grasp onto that thought, it starts to change.
It's changing anyway, whether we think that or not.
We hold something, and then it starts to crumble.
It starts to change.
Then we say, "Oh, but wait a minute, don't go away."
And it continues to change.
Then it starts to get painful, and we're not happy.
We want to hold onto that state of mind.
But as soon as we hold onto it, we start to suffer.
Try to be aware when you have a good feeling like that, and just enjoy it.
When it starts to change, just let it go.
When you're not open to everything, you suffer.
Dogen said, "Flowers fall with our attachment."
We want something so bad, and yet the flower falls, and weeds spring up.
It is difficult.
It is hard to be open to what you would ordinarily be averse to.
It's counterintuitive.
When we have pain or discomfort, we usually want to change it.
As Suzuki Roshi said,*
we're continually changing our equipment, moving around, trying to get comfortable.
As soon as we get comfortable, it changes and becomes uncomfortable.
This is how things are.
The way to be comfortable, to have true comfort, is not through trying to control the world around us, but to adjust to ourself, to open ourselves from the inside.
When we open ourselves from the inside, absolute and relative are transcended.
Subject and object are no longer duality, and we can accept various states of body and mind without being a victim.
So thank you, Sojun Mel Weitsman.
I took that as a good segue to the next four lines.
*The person in the hut lives calmly, not stuck to inside, outside, or in between.
Places worldly people live, he doesn't live.
Realms worldly people love, he doesn't love.*
Let's open up for any first comments people have about these lines and how they might reflect on what we've just considered about the hut and the weeds and the person living there.
Well, I've been working on trying not to get so tangled up when I get upset about politics, trying not to feed that and other things.
The line "not stuck to inside, outside, or in between" really registered with me, because what came up was just to flow.
If I get upset, okay, just be upset, but watch it and let it move instead of grabbing onto it and feeding it.
That was really quite helpful.

Then I was reading a part of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, where Suzuki Roshi talked about the way to control an animal, a sheep or a horse, is to give them a big pasture, which means just let them roam.
So let your thoughts arise, watch them and let them go when it's time to go, but don't try to hold on or contain them or get rid of them or any of that.
It felt very similar to "not stuck to inside, outside, or in between."
So that really touched on what I've been working on.
Good.
A lot of thoughts?
Yeah, along what John is saying, I had an aha moment on page 45, second full paragraph.
He says:
*There's an odd thing.

If we turn to look inside and focus on seeing thoughts and emotions, rather than being caught by them and believing the stories they tell us, those very things that we thought were us, ourself or our inside, become object of our consciousness, things that we observe.
They are now outside.*
I hadn't really considered how permeable that inside-outside state is.
It almost sounds like there really isn't much of a barrier between inside and outside.
That leads me into the thought that we are all one, and it makes that a lot more real for me.
So I was real thankful for that.
Another comment?
Thought?
Yeah, in my own practice, I have to learn over and over again.

There's so much impulse to try to pick the weeds and remove the weeds, and I need to learn the lesson over and over: I want to pick the weeds to open the space in my mind, but it's actually when I just allow the weeds that the space can open up.
Then any grasping for that space just creates new weeds.
So it's to sit with it without any preference.
That seems like what this is pointing to.

One perspective that seemed to make sense to me: I was reading these passages and had been looking for other reasons that the Lotus Sutra came across, and I found a passage in chapter 14 that calls safe and easy practice.
It says:
*A bodhisattva takes a stand on perseverance and is never alarmed in mind.
And with regard to phenomena, he takes no action, but observes the true entity of phenomena without acting or making any distinction.
This is called the practice of a bodhisattva.*
So I think that's the same sort of thing as John's stepping back and observing without being attached to that observation.

Ben points out that one of the things that happens in this first line of this passage is that all of a sudden we've gone from "I built the hut" to now "the person in the hut," which shifts perspective from the first person to the third person.
He proposes that that pronoun shift indicates a letting go of attachment to the individual, a moving to a state of calm abiding.
If there's an aspect to our practice, it's to find that place of tranquility, of peacefulness, of calmness.
Whenever I think about living calmly, there's a great line that Robert Aitken loves from Wallace Stevens, where he says:
*The day is like wide water without sound.*
That notion of living calmly, that image, is a really helpful place to keep coming back to.

John mentioned, and Scott as well, not being stuck to inside, one could say not being stuck to meditation; not being stuck to outside, to the rules or expectations of others; not being stuck to in between, not being stuck on meditation, not being stuck on our calmness, but realizing that that changes too.
One of Sherdu's one-liners that is helpful, I think, is:
*What the eye sees is the way.
What the eye sees is the way.
And what the eye sees is not separate, it is all mind.*
To me, the operative word in that sentence is the "stuck" word, not the inside, the outside or in between, but the stuck part.
It's the attachment to a condition.
So to me, this line really speaks to a lesson on non-attachment, and even not an attachment to thinking we have to meditate.
The attachment is to any notion of structure or content that our minds bring forward.

Let me read another passage from the Lotus Sutra, the same section, because I think it ties right to this "not stuck to inside, outside, or in between," and right back to what John was speaking to as well.
*Moreover, one should not hold to things as higher, middle or lower, constituted or unconstituted, real or unreal.
One should not seek to grasp things, know them or see them.
All things are empty and without being, without permanence, neither arising nor ending.
This is called that with which wise people associate.
In a quiet place, one can master one's mind and heart, dwelling as peacefully and unmoved as Mount Sumeru, regarding all things as non-substantial, like empty space without solidity.*
*Places worldly people live, he doesn't live.
Realms worldly people love, he doesn't love.*
This seems to be addressing the social aspects of withdrawing from the world.
Here he is in his hermitage on top of this rock, in his grass hut, and he's not hanging out with anybody.
Let's take a minute and reflect on what that's telling us, what we bring forth from those lines.
I have a comment.
I think of the historic part of where Sherdu built his temple, and it was a very popular place.
There were many temples up there, or at least a number of them, and they were quite beautiful, and he was invited to inhabit one of them, and he chose not to.
So that would, to me, be the worldly people.
At least on a really snapshot look at all these temples and then this little grass hut, he was really living that.
Twenty-two years.
The rest just points back to admonishments we get in our practice from so many of the things we read, where we're reminded that we don't have to have riches.
We don't have to have the outside comforts that we may desire to have a rich life.
Other thoughts, comments?
Yeah.

I was thinking about this idea of shifting from the first to the third person, and what occurred to me is that it's like when you're telling somebody about a dream that you've had: "Well, I was there, but then I was looking at it from over here."
Parts of the poem really give me the sense that I almost feel like I'm interpreting a dream.
That dreamlike shift, for me, was the paradox that it can be both ways.
Then that was tying into the idea that we're both separate, but we're also really interconnected.
So that's where I was going with that line.
I had that same thought as I was struggling with the shift from first person to third person.
It occurred to me, as I was wrestling with that, that he was napping.
He said that from the beginning and perhaps never woke up from his nap.
Maybe everything else is a dream sequence.
On the first to third person, just a curiosity, Bob: would you talk to your Chinese scholar friend about that?
I found myself wondering, and I know it's addressed in the commentary to some extent, but I wonder if he had some additional thoughts about ruling out translation issues or linguistic anomalies.
No, and in fact, in this passage, "person" is the pronoun.
Later on, there's actually a place where Ben keeps the translation as the third person, where he shakes back to the first person.
But in this passage, definitely third person.
It says "person."
It's the two-legged kind of character.
If you look at the front of the book, where we see a two-legged character, it's a person.
So it's third person for sure.
It seems like the shift from first person to third person could represent the shift in identity from the self to no self, or a shift from the perspective of the relative to the absolute.
In the first paragraph, where there's the identity with the self or the perspective of the relative, that's covered with weeds.
Illusion.
And in the third paragraph, if this represents a shift to no self or the absolute, the person in the hut lives calmly without any preference.

I think that's what Ben is inferring: that it's moving to letting go of attachment to the individual, just seeing himself as just another person in this hut, and his attachment, his connection to himself, is gone.
It's simply another phenomenon in the world.
One of the interesting aspects, of course, of Sherdu being a hermit is withdrawing by choice, and these passages about realms and worldly people.

Generally speaking, those who were hermits, if they were educated, became hermits because they decided to, or because they weren't able to get a job with the government, and government jobs were in these worldly places.
When he talks about palaces and towers, that's where you would live if you were a well-trained person in China at that time.
So one sense is of stepping back from urban life.
One of the things that struck me is that in our, I'll call them city lives, we still have choices about where we spend our time and our attention.
I came across one of my favorite philosophers, a Negro League pitcher named Satchel Page.
Satchel Page has some great aphorisms, and one of them is: "Go very light on the vices, such as carrying on in society.
The social ramble ain't restful."
I think one of the messages here is that if you want to have peace and be calm, being involved in the world at large in society is probably not the recipe that you want to follow.
So one of the questions is how we find that calm place in our rambling lives, because we all live a rambling life with the interactions and people we intersect with.

But I wanted to bring a different perspective to bear on this, where he's living is a line that I just took as a meditation koan from the Diamond Sutra, from the passage that reads, *don't dwell upon colors to bring forth the mind, don't dwell upon phenomena of sound, smell, taste or touch to bring forth the mind, dwell nowhere and bring forth that mind.* When he talks about living, we could use the synonyms "to dwell" or "to stay."
To me, one of the messages here goes back to that stuck notion earlier, that we have a choice.

Robert Aitken, in an essay of his on the [unclear: "mind of Klobriko"], bringing forth the mind, calls it living the unborn: the mind that doesn't dwell upon phenomena, that experiences the inside and the outside, the inner and the outer, as one.
So actually dwelling everywhere and nowhere and then bringing forth that mind is part of our task, part of our opportunity when we sit and practice.
It means not rejecting anything, or clinging or attaching to anything.
It means a kind of spaciousness.
It means each moment we have an attitude of openness and acceptance.
In a sense, it's very much parallel to and complementary to the issues we were talking about, the grass hut and the weeds.
This is really: where do we choose to live?
But it also raises a question I raised to you, which is: if this person doesn't live where others do and doesn't love what others love, where does he or she live and what does he or she love?
So let me throw that question out, turning his statement inside out.
Where is this person living and what is he loving, or she?
In that line too, it's not saying where other people live or what other people love.
It's where worldly people live and worldly people love.

So I don't read it necessarily as being isolated or apart from all others, but I hear it a little bit as not living or loving in that realm of keeping up with others or comparing with others what they're doing.
Should I be doing more?
Should I be doing less and wanting to be above average?
It's just letting that go, stepping back from that somewhat.
Other thoughts out there?
I just want to read out from the chat because Kerry put something there.
Not stuck to inside, outside or in between.
I appreciate Ben's commentary.
Whatever is right here now is what we have to work with.
So our hermit just works with what he has and doesn't need what the worldly people love or where they live, I guess.
We're getting back to what Bob had said earlier: what the eye sees is the way.
I'm just quite sure.
I don't have that kind of wisdom.
And where is that?
That's from his sayings?
Yeah, yeah.
You're talking about inside, outside or in between.
That got back to the change in person from first person to third person.
First person is "I," which is the observer, and all he does is change to the third person, which is outside of him, which is the observed.
So the only thing that really changes is, it's still the same narrative, but the point of view changes.
One way he's looking from self out and the other way he's looking from other back to the self.
So it's pretty much the same thing, only the point of view changes.
It'd be like that a few pages down the road.
He was talking about the mule looking down the well and the well looking back at the mule.
It's similar to what he says a little later on about the mule looking down at the well and then the well is looking back at the mule.
So it's a similar thing where you have an entity looking from both directions and the center is anybody's guess.
I really don't have a handle on that.
Are there thoughts out there?
If not, maybe, want to do breakout rooms?
Yeah, I have a couple of questions for people to consider.
So we'll take 10 minutes and go into breakout rooms, and I think we'll actually have a few minutes to have people say a few things if they care to when they come back.
So, three questions, take any one or all of them.
First one is: how do we recognize and embrace our impermanence and the emergence of difficulties?
Second is: where do we live really?
Where do we live and how do we live?
And the third is: how much are we driven by social expectations, internal dialogues of achieving something, even perfection or enlightenment, as Tallis's talk on Sunday was focused on?
How much are we driven by our internal dialogue about achievement and reaching some point?
And let's take those questions and go to breakout rooms.
So again, Bob, you're going to bounce around a little bit there.
How do we recognize and embrace our impermanence?
Where do we live really, and how?
How much are we driven by social expectations and internal dialogue?
And maybe in the future, we can put these up in the chat room.
I'm sorry, we're learning this technology.
I got your back, Bob.
Thanks, Tim.
Oh, please stay tuned for breakout rooms.
Let's see.
Just a moment.
Whoops.
Did it?
Do you see?
Are there people in different rooms?
Looks like room one is everybody.
I'm fearful that I've not put people into what they need.
Oh, dear.
I hope you're all enjoying this gaffe.
Okay.
John was on a run there.
I'd like to hear what [unclear: "Delph John"] had to say.
Okay, go for it.
It just seems like with many things in Buddhism, you try what Buddhism recommends.
You try to approach things in that way, and does that reduce your suffering or not?
Are we better off to come to terms with impermanence and learn how to live with it and see it and accept it?
Does that cause less suffering?
Or are we better off acting like it's not going to happen?
I know the answer for me.
I know that answer to that question.
But I think we all have to make that decision for ourselves.
Certainly, our culture recommends pretending impermanence doesn't exist.
As they say, you can run but you can't hide, John.
And as you get older, you can't run very fast.
He's exactly not running.
He's relaxing in the hut.
Speaking as a gardener, I find that every fall season that comes is a reminder of impermanence.
You see things that you loved in the summer, they flourished, and then they wither and pass away.
And always, the fall is special to me for that recognition of how things come to a close.
I want to say that for me, one of the most dramatic impressions of impermanence has come from aging.
When you reach 70, it seems like things start really to change really fast.
At first there's this feeling like, oh, tomorrow I'm not going to feel this way.
Tomorrow I'm going to feel like I was when I was 40 or even 50.
But that doesn't happen.
After a while, you begin to recognize that.
You recognize, yeah, next month is going to be different, and another five years from now is going to be really different.
So that's been a real lesson for me in impermanence.
Are there other thoughts out there?
Are there other images that were triggered by these lines?
I'm just thinking about your question about where do we live, really.
In some ways, we live in the outside world, like in our homes, where we go to work, where we shop, walking down the street.
In other ways we live in our internal world, with our thoughts and our feelings.
And then there's that in-between, because we integrate those.
So I think that goes along a lot with his thing about not being stuck to inside, outside or in between.
Let me move between all of those.
A comment on how we embrace impermanence: I would suggest that I embrace impermanence every time I feel fear or anxiety.
I find that that's usually connected to, why is there fear?
It's probably connected to impermanence, or possibly something going wrong, or being safe.
That's what's come up for me in that respect.
It's recognizing impermanence when we're unconscious of it.
That's to me the challenge.
I'm really interested in what Claire said in terms of sangha life.

I wonder if what we love about coming together to the zendo, whether it's real or virtual, is that we're all setting aside our usual external world and entering into a shared zendo world where our internal world can be more present, or something like that.
I want to think about that some more, but I thought that was interesting, what you said, Claire.
Something occurs to me about both impermanence and where and how we live.
